extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining novelty/anticipation, public use, on-sale bars, and ways to overcome pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/(b) rejections, including range/genus-species issues, derivation/affidavits, and continuation-in-part filing-date rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific prior-art example within claimed range anticipates the range
rubrics_metrics.description: "[W]hen, as by a recitation of ranges or otherwise, a claim covers several compositions, the claim is 'anticipated' if one of them is in the prior art." (Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner; In re Petering example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art reference contains a specific example/data point that falls within a claimed numerical/chemical range, that reference anticipates the claimed range. Example: a plotted data point corresponding to a composition within the claimed range is an anticipating disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping or touching prior-art ranges anticipate only with 'sufficient specificity'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prior art discloses a range that touches or overlaps the claimed range but does not provide specific examples within the claimed range, anticipation depends on whether the reference discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' to constitute an anticipation under the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a case-by-case inquiry. Consider: breadth of the claimed vs reference range, presence or absence of evidence of criticality, whether the patentee showed the claimed range is critical, and whether one of ordinary skill would expect different results outside the claimed range. Compare ClearValue (anticipatory where no criticality shown) and Atofina (not anticipatory where claimed range shown to be critical). If specificity is unclear, examiner may make a combined §102/§103 analysis and must provide reasons for anticipation and a reasoned statement on obviousness (Ex parte Lee). Unexpected results within the narrow range may bear on nonobviousness (see MPEP § 716.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art values very close but not overlapping do not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Anticipation under §102 can be found only when the reference discloses exactly what is claimed ..." (Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art's value/range is very close to but does not overlap/touch the claimed range, it does not anticipate; differences between the reference and the claim must be addressed under §103 (obviousness) rather than §102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations are irrelevant to §102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations, such as unexpected results or commercial success, is irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections and thus cannot overcome a rejection so based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need, unexpected results) may be relevant to obviousness (§103) but are not a defense to a novelty (§102) rejection. See In re Wiggins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous art or 'teaches away' arguments are not germane to anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that the alleged anticipatory prior art is 'nonanalogous art' or 'teaches away from the invention' are not germane to a rejection under section 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference may anticipate even if it addresses a different problem, is from a different field, disparages the invention, or teaches away. The relevant question for anticipation is whether the reference explicitly or inherently discloses every limitation of the claim. See Twin Disc, Celeritas, Upsher-Smith, Atlas Powder examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory elements of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a): A person shall be entitled to a patent unless the invention was known or used by others in this country, or patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country, before the invention thereof by the applicant for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory text frames anticipation/public-use analysis under pre-AIA law; subsequent MPEP guidance explains how to apply each element (known/used, in this country, by others, patented/printed publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Known or used' requires public accessibility (no deliberate secrecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The statutory language 'known or used by others in this country' ... means knowledge or use which is accessible to the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A use is publicly accessible if there was no deliberate attempt to keep it secret. Sales of products made by a secret process are public uses only if the process can be determined by examining the product; otherwise secret process use plus sales may not be a public use. See Carella; W. L. Gore & Assoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: "In this country' means the United States (pre-AIA 102(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Only knowledge or use in the U.S. can be used in a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection; foreign-only knowledge/use cannot be the basis for such a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NAFTA/URAA changes to 35 U.S.C. 104 do not modify the meaning of 'in this country' for pre-AIA 102(a). See In re Ekenstam.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'By others' means any entity different from the inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'others' in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) refers to any entity which is different from the inventive entity; the entity need only differ by one person to be 'by others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to all types of prior art references (publications, public knowledge/use). This interpretation preserves the 1-year grace period under §102(b). See In re Katz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 102(a) rejection by persuasively arguing patentable distinction, amending claims, submitting certain affidavits/declarations, or perfecting priority/benefit claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible approaches listed include: (A) arguing claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) amending claims; (C) filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit showing prior invention (when reference is not a U.S. patent/publication with interfering subject matter); (D) filing a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit showing reference disclosure was derived from the inventor (derivation); (E) submitting and perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); (F) submitting and perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120. See MPEP § 2132.01 and §715 for affidavit requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements and limits for disclaiming/derivation affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference's authorship includes the inventor or a joint inventor, the reference may be removed as a prior art reference by filing a disclaiming affidavit/declaration establishing that the relevant portions originated with the inventor or joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaiming affidavits or 1.132 declarations must provide context, explanation, and evidence — a naked assertion of inventorship is insufficient. Cases: In re Katz (research-paper co-authorship context where declarations and facts supported sole inventorship); EmeraChem (insufficient bare declaration); Ex parte Kroger (conflicting evidence from coauthor prevented overcoming rejection). Adding coauthors as joint inventors is an alternative if requirements of 35 U.S.C. 116 are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit can antedate references to overcome 102(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit may be used to antedate a non-statutory-bar reference (i.e., show prior invention) and thereby overcome a pre-AIA 102(a) rejection in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use is limited where the reference is a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claiming interfering subject matter—then 1.131 is not appropriate. When the reference discloses inventor's own work, either a 1.131 (antedating) or 1.132 (derivation) may be submitted depending on circumstances. See In re Foster; In re Facius; MPEP §715 for required evidence to support 1.131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1-year grace period under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and extension rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications, patents, public uses and sales must occur 'more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States' to bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b). If the 1-year period would otherwise end on a holiday or weekend, it is extended to the next working day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-year bar is measured from the U.S. filing date. Rule changes recognizing deposit dates (e.g., Priority Express Mail) do not affect an applicant's right to defer filing to the next business day when the last day falls on a weekend/holiday. See Ex parte Olah and MPEP §2133.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date for CIPs is claim-by-claim (CIP rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date of a claimed invention is determined on a claim-by-claim basis; claims not supported by the parent have the filing date of the child CIP, and prior art more than 1 year before that child's filing date can bar patentability under 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims fully supported by the parent retain the parent's filing date; claims containing limitations only supported by the CIP have the CIP's filing date. See Santarus v. Par Pharm.; Studiengesellschaft Kohle v. Shell Oil; MPEP §2133.01 and §2139.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's own pre-grace-period disclosures can be used as 102(b) prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: "Any invention described in a printed publication more than one year prior to the date of a patent application is prior art under Section 102(b), even if the printed publication was authored by the patent applicant." (De Graffenried; Bonito Boats quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once an inventor publicly discloses the invention more than one year before filing, the inventor is barred from patenting that subject matter. Such a 102(b) bar cannot be overcome by affidavits/declarations showing prior invention or derivation, nor by foreign priority dates. See In re Foster and MPEP §2133.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 102(b) rejection by arguing patentable distinction, amending claims, or perfecting certain priority/benefit claims (35 U.S.C. 120, 119(e), 119(a)-(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically listed options include: (A) argue patentable distinction; (B) amend claims; (C) submit and perfect a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 (with correct ADS or specification amendment and showing enablement/written description), (D) submit and perfect benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e). If perfected, reconsider whether the prior art becomes pre-AIA 102(a) or remains 102(b). PLTIA restoration provisions may apply for late provisional benefit under certain conditions. See MPEP §2133.02(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use and on-sale bars are distinct components of 102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) contains several distinct bars to patentability, including public use and on-sale bars; either may apply when the other does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use may exist without sales; conversely, there may be a secret sale or offer to sell that still constitutes a statutory bar. The analyses for public use and on-sale differ and both affect how an inventor may use the invention prior to filing. See Dart Indus. and Hobbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy considerations underlying public-use and on-sale bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies include (A) encouraging prompt disclosure of inventions via patents; (B) preventing commercial exploitation of exclusivity beyond the statutory period; (C) discouraging removal of inventions from the public domain that the public believes are freely available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These policy rationales inform interpretation and application of the public-use and on-sale bars. See RCA Corp. v. Data Gen.; Manville Sales Corp. v. Paramount Sys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for 'public use' under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper test for the public use prong is whether the purported use: (1) was accessible to the public; or (2) was commercially exploited. Commercial exploitation is a clear indication of public use, but it likely requires more than, for example, a secret offer for sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applying the test consider evidence relevant to experimentation, nature of the activity that occurred in public, public access to the use, confidentiality obligations imposed on observers, and commercial exploitation. This evidence is relevant to whether the use was a public use that could raise a bar, but is distinct from evidence relevant to 'ready for patenting' under Pfaff's two-part test. See Invitrogen Corp. v. Biocrest and MPEP §2133.03(c).
